'''''Triplaris americana''''' is a species of flowering plant in the [[Polygonaceae|knotweed family]] known by many common names, including '''ant tree'''<ref name=pier>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/triplaris_americana.htm ''Triplaris americana''.] Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk.</ref> or '''''pau-formiga''''' ("ant tree"),<ref name=had>Haddad Junior, V., et al. (2009). [http://www.scielo.br/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0037-86822009000600022 The Triplaria tree (''Triplaris'' spp) and ''Pseudomyrmex'' ants: a symbiotic relationship with risks of attack for humans.] ''Revista da Sociedade Brasileira de Medicina Tropical'' 42 6.</ref> '''''guacamayo''''', '''''guayabo zancón''''', '''''hormiguero''''', '''''palo de Santa María''''', '''''tachí''''', '''''vara santa''''',<ref name=col>[http://www.siac.net.co/sib/catalogoespecies/especie.do;jsessionid=EBFBB7433FFCB86D70A2D91425812725?idBuscar=1400&method=displayAAT ''Triplaris americana''.] Catálogo de la Biodiversidad de Colombia.</ref> '''''pau-de-novato''''', '''''formigueiro''''', '''''taxizeiro'','''<ref name="had" /> and '''devil tree'''.<ref>{{Cite book |title=1491 : new revelations of the Americas before Columbus |last=Mann, Charles C. |date=2005 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=9781400040063 |edition=1st |location=New York |oclc=56632601 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/1491newrevelatio00mann }}</ref> It is native to [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]], occurring from [[Panama]] to [[Brazil]].<ref name=pier/> It is also cultivated as an [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] for its showy pink flowers.<ref name=sapia>[http://www.arc.agric.za/uploads/images/0_SAPIA_NEWS_No._15.PDF Ant tree (''Triplaris americana'') is: Beautiful.......but dangerous!.]{{Dead link|date=July 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=no }} Southern African Plant Invaders Atlas, April 2010.</ref>

The ant tree grows up to 30 meters in height, with a trunk up to 30 centimeters in diameter and [[ochrea]] up to 12 centimeters in length. Its smooth bark is a mottled gray color. The leaves are oval to oblong and measure up to 40 centimeters long by 20 wide, with undersides that are sometimes woolly with brown fibers. The male flowers are around 2 millimeters long, while the female flowers are up to 5 centimeters long.<ref name=pier/> This tree is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], and has a skewed [[sex ratio]] with many more female plants than male.<ref name=mel>Melampy, M. N. and H. F. Howe. (1977). [http://www.uic.edu/labs/howe/pdfs/MelampyHoweEvol77.pdf Sex ratio in the tropical tree ''Triplaris americana'' (Polygonaceae).] ''Evolution'' 31 867-72.</ref>

This tree grows in [[river|riparian]] habitat types, and is a colonizer of disturbed habitat.<ref name=mel/> It has been introduced to areas outside its native range, including [[Hawaii]]<ref name=pier/> and southern [[Africa]].<ref name=sapia/>

This species of tree is a [[myrmecophyte]] and it has a [[mutualism (biology)|mutualistic relationship]] with [[ant]]s, including ''[[Pseudomyrmex triplarinus]]''. This kind of ant lives within the tree, feeding on substances produced by it and defending it against invaders.<ref name=bak>Bakalar, N. [https://www.nytimes.com/2011/05/17/science/17obants.html Polite guests, ants pick host trees out of a crowd.] ''New York Times'' May 13, 2011.</ref> This tree is known as a "novice tree" (''pau-de-novato'') because only one unfamiliar with the tree would touch it, soon discovering that the ants are aggressive and venomous.<ref name=had/>

This tree is considered a [[noxious weed]] in southern Africa.<ref name=pier/> The fruits are [[seed dispersal|dispersed]] on the wind and the seedlings easily take hold and become [[invasive species|invasive]], growing in the local habitat and displacing native plants.<ref name=sapia/>
